questions.question: The conjugate base of the ammonium ion is
questions.answer: A conjugate base is formed when an acid donates a proton: $\text{NH}_4^+\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3+\text{H}^+$. The conjugate base of $\text{NH}_4^+$ is $\text{NH}_3$.

questions.question: Which of the equations below is correct for the reaction of sulfuric acid and aluminium carbonate solid?
questions.answer: Aluminium carbonate is $\text{Al}_2(\text{CO}_3)_3$ (Al$^{3+}$ and CO$_3^{2-}$) and, being a solid, is written $(s)$. An acid plus a carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide: $\text{Al}_2(\text{CO}_3)_3(s)+3\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)\rightarrow\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+3\text{CO}_2(g)$, which is balanced (2 Al, 3 S, 3 C, 6 H and 21 O on each side). Options A and C use the wrong formula for aluminium carbonate, and B gives the solid the wrong state.

questions.question: What is the solubility of $\text{MgF}_2$ ($K_{sp}=6.8\times10^{-9}$) in pure water?
questions.answer:
$\text{MgF}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{F}^-(aq)$. If the solubility is $s$, $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]=s$ and $[\text{F}^-]=2s$:
$$K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3\Rightarrow s=\sqrt[3]{\frac{6.8\times10^{-9}}4}=1.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: The diagram shows the behaviour of two different acids when they are dissolved in distilled water (each beaker shows the acid before and after dissolving; the key distinguishes undissociated acid molecules, dissociated positive ions and dissociated negative ions). Which row of the table correctly describes the two acids?
questions.answer: Strength describes the extent of ionisation, not the amount of acid. In the diagram acid X remains mostly as undissociated molecules with only a few ions formed, so it is a weak acid, whereas acid Y has almost all of its molecules dissociated into ions, so it is a strong acid. (Concentrated and dilute describe the amount of acid per volume, which cannot be judged from this diagram.)
options: Acid X: concentrated; Acid Y: dilute
Acid X: dilute; Acid Y: concentrated
Acid X: strong; Acid Y: weak
Acid X: weak; Acid Y: strong

questions.question: How many different structural isomers are there for $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{BrCl}$?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{BrCl}$ is a saturated (propane) skeleton with one Br and one Cl replacing two H atoms. Possibilities: both on C1 (1-bromo-1-chloropropane); both on C2 (2-bromo-2-chloropropane); on C1 and C2 in two ways (1-bromo-2-chloropropane and 2-bromo-1-chloropropane); on C1 and C3 (1-bromo-3-chloropropane). That gives 5.

questions.question: How many products are possible when but-2-ene reacts with $\text{HCl}(g)$?
questions.answer: But-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, is symmetrical about its double bond, so adding H and Cl across it gives the same structure whichever carbon the Cl attaches to: only 2-chlorobutane is formed (1 product).

questions.question: Nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, has $K_a=4.5\times10^{-4}$. What is the best description of the species present in a $0.1$ M solution of nitrous acid?
questions.answer: $K_a$ is small ($4.5\times10^{-4}$), so $\text{HNO}_2$ is a weak acid that ionises only slightly: $[\text{H}^+]\approx\sqrt{4.5\times10^{-4}\times0.1}=6.7\times10^{-3}$ M, i.e. only about $7\%$ ionised. The predominant species is therefore undissociated $\text{HNO}_2$.
options: $\text{HNO}_2(aq)$ is the predominant species; much smaller amounts of $\text{H}^+(aq)$ and $\text{NO}_2^-(aq)$ are present.
$\text{H}^+(aq)$ and $\text{NO}_2^-(aq)$ are the predominant species; much smaller amounts of $\text{HNO}_2(aq)$ are present.
Only $\text{H}^+(aq)$ and $\text{NO}_2^-(aq)$ are present in measurable amounts.
$\text{HNO}_2(aq)$, $\text{H}^+(aq)$ and $\text{NO}_2^-(aq)$ are all present in comparable amounts.

questions.question: For the reaction $\text{Br}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{IBr}(g)$, $K_{eq}=1.2\times10^2$ at $150^\circ$C. Given this, what is $K_{eq}$ for the reaction $4\text{IBr}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{Br}_2(g)+2\text{I}_2(g)$ at $150^\circ$C?
questions.answer:
Reversing the equation inverts $K$, and doubling the coefficients squares it:
$$K'=\left(\frac1{1.2\times10^2}\right)^2=\frac1{14400}=6.9\times10^{-5}.$$

questions.question: A student wants to use a physical property to distinguish between two alcohols, octan-1-ol and propan-1-ol. Both alcohols are colourless liquids at standard laboratory conditions. The student should use,
questions.answer: Octan-1-ol has a much longer non-polar carbon chain, so stronger dispersion forces between molecules, and therefore a much higher boiling point ($195^\circ$C vs $97^\circ$C). Densities are similar, neither alcohol conducts electricity, and the longer-chain octan-1-ol is less (not more) soluble in water.
options: density because propan-1-ol has a much higher density than octan-1-ol.
boiling point because octan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than propan-1-ol.
electrical conductivity because octan-1-ol has a higher conductivity than propan-1-ol.
solubility because octan-1-ol will have a higher solubility in water than propan-1-ol.

questions.question: A compound with the formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$ has the following features: it is unbranched; it has only one type of functional group; all carbon-to-carbon bonds are single bonds. The compound could be classified as an
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$ has one degree of unsaturation (a saturated acyclic $\text{C}_6$ compound with two O would be $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$). With all C–C bonds single, the unsaturation must be a C=O double bond, and with two oxygen atoms and one type of functional group the compound is an ester (or a carboxylic acid, which is not offered), e.g. ethyl butanoate. An amide needs nitrogen, and an alcohol or aldehyde with this formula would need a second, different functional group (or a ring or branch).

questions.question:
$X$ is prepared from the reaction of $Y$ and $Z$ as described in the following equation:
$$\text{Y}(g)+\text{Z}(g)\rightleftharpoons3\text{X}(g)\qquad\Delta H=-50\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Which set of conditions would increase the rate at which $X(g)$ is initially produced?
questions.answer:
The question asks about the **rate**, not the equilibrium yield. By collision theory, increasing the pressure of gases increases their concentration so there are more collisions per second, and increasing the temperature increases the proportion of collisions with energy above the activation energy (and the collision frequency). Both increase the rate of the forward reaction, so high pressure and high temperature give the fastest initial rate (option A). (Low temperature or low pressure would favour the yield of $X$ in terms of equilibrium position for the exothermic forward reaction, but would slow the reaction.)

*School error:* the school's answer sheet gives B (low pressure, low temperature), which would give the slowest rate.

questions.question: Which of the molecules below is a functional group isomer of butanoic acid?
questions.answer: Butanoic acid is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ (a carboxylic acid). A functional group isomer has the same molecular formula but a different functional group. Structure D is ethyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, an ester with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$. A is butanone ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$), B is butane-2,3-diol ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$) and C is butanal ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$): none has the correct formula.

questions.question:
The table shows $pK_{ind}$, the pH range, and the colour changes of three indicators.

| Indicator | $pK_{ind}$ | pH range | Colour at lower pH | Colour at higher pH |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bromophenol blue | 4.0 | 3.0 – 4.6 | yellow | blue |
| methyl red | 5.1 | 4.2 – 6.3 | red | yellow |
| phenolphthalein | 9.3 | 8.3 – 10.0 | colourless | red |

At a pH of 4, which option correctly identifies the colour of the solution with each indicator?
questions.answer: At pH 4: bromophenol blue is within its range (3.0–4.6), near its $pK_{ind}$ of 4.0, so both forms are present and the colour is the mixture, green. Methyl red's range begins at 4.2, so at pH 4 (below the range) it is in its low-pH colour, red. Phenolphthalein is far below its range, so it is colourless.
options: Bromophenol blue: yellow; methyl red: red; phenolphthalein: colourless
Bromophenol blue: yellow; methyl red: yellow; phenolphthalein: colourless
Bromophenol blue: green; methyl red: orange; phenolphthalein: colourless
Bromophenol blue: green; methyl red: red; phenolphthalein: colourless

questions.question: A student is told that an unlabelled solution may contain one or more nitrate salts of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ and/or $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. They are required to determine which cation(s) are present and are provided with several solid ionic compounds for this analysis. Which compound below, when added to water, would form an effective reagent for the first step in this analysis?
questions.answer: The first step should precipitate only one of the possible cations, so that the others can be tested separately. Chloride precipitates only $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ($\text{PbCl}_2$ is insoluble; $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{BaCl}_2$ are soluble). Silver chloride is insoluble, so it will not form a solution reagent. Sulfate precipitates both $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (PbSO$_4$ and BaSO$_4$ are insoluble), so lithium sulfate and copper(II) sulfate are not selective. Potassium chloride is the effective reagent.

questions.question:
The tetrachlorocopper(II) anion forms a green solution and reacts with water to form the blue hexaaquacopper(II) cation according to the following equation:
$$\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\qquad\Delta H=\text{negative}$$
At a constant pressure and temperature, the appearance of a solution containing these ions remains pale blue. Which alternative correctly predicts an identified change and its effect on the system?
questions.answer:
Concentrated HCl adds $\text{Cl}^-$ ions (a product), so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts left, forming more green $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$: the solution turns green. Diluting with water favours the side with more dissolved particles (the right), so it would become bluer, not green (A is wrong). Cooling decreases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions (B is wrong). The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium left, producing more green $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ (C is wrong).

*School error:* the school's answer sheet gives C, but heating an exothermic forward reaction favours the reverse reaction and a greener solution.
options: Adding water causes the solution to turn green.
Cooling the reaction vessel increases the rate of the reverse reaction.
Increasing the temperature causes the solution to turn blue.
Adding concentrated hydrochloric acid causes the solution to turn green.

questions.question: The structure of an organic compound is shown: $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{COOH}$ (but-2-enoic acid). What mass of chlorine molecules would react completely with $0.250$ moles of the compound?
questions.answer: Only the C=C double bond reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ (addition), 1 mol $\text{Cl}_2$ per mol compound. $n(\text{Cl}_2)=0.250$ mol, $m=0.250\times70.90=17.73$ g.

questions.question: The curve shows the change in pH against the volume of solution added from a burette during an acid–base titration (the pH starts at about 11, falls gradually to about 7.5, then drops sharply at about $28$ mL to about 2). Which alternative identifies the type of solution present in the conical flask and burette during this titration?
questions.answer: The pH starts high (about 11) and decreases, so the flask contains a base and the burette an acid. The initial pH (about 11) is well below that of a strong base of similar concentration (about 13), and the gradual buffer region followed by an equivalence point below pH 7 shows the flask contains a weak base. The steep final drop to a low pH (about 2) shows the acid added is strong.
options: Flask: strong base; burette: strong acid
Flask: weak base; burette: strong acid
Flask: weak acid; burette: weak base
Flask: strong acid; burette: weak base

questions.question: A student mixed $10.0$ mL of $0.0400\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with $40.0$ mL of $0.35\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ KOH. What is the pH of the resulting solution?

The structural formulae of five organic compounds, labelled A–E, are shown: A methyl propanoate, B ethyl ethanoate, C 2-methylpropanoic acid, D propyl methanoate, E butanoic acid (all $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$). Which alternative below identifies a pair of these compounds which are examples of each type of structural isomer?
questions.answer: Chain isomers have the same functional group but a differently branched carbon chain: C (branched acid) and E (straight-chain acid). Functional group isomers have different functional groups: an ester and a carboxylic acid, such as A and C. Position isomers have the same functional group in a different position: B and D (both esters, with the ester linkage $-\text{COO}-$ at a different position along the carbon skeleton). This is option A.
options: Chain: C and E; functional group: A and C; position: B and D
Chain: A and C; functional group: A and E; position: A and D
Chain: E and C; functional group: A and B; position: B and E
Chain: D and E; functional group: B and C; position: A and B

questions.question: Compare and contrast the relative solubility of lead(II) hydroxide and lead(II) phosphate. (From the data sheet: $K_{sp}(\text{Pb(OH)}_2)=1.43\times10^{-15}$ and $K_{sp}(\text{Pb}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2)=8.0\times10^{-43}$.)
questions.answer: Both compounds have very small $K_{sp}$ values ($1.43\times10^{-15}$ and $8.0\times10^{-43}$), so both are only very slightly soluble in water. However, $\text{Pb}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$ has a far smaller $K_{sp}$ than $\text{Pb(OH)}_2$, so lead(II) phosphate is much less soluble than lead(II) hydroxide. (Check: $s=\sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}=7\times10^{-6}$ mol L$^{-1}$ for $\text{Pb(OH)}_2$ and $s=\sqrt[5]{K_{sp}/108}=1.5\times10^{-9}$ mol L$^{-1}$ for $\text{Pb}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$, so the same conclusion holds when the different formulas are taken into account.)

questions.question: The solubility product, $K_{sp}$, of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is $6.4\times10^{-6}$ at 298 K. Calculate the solubility (in g L$^{-1}$) of calcium hydroxide in pure water at 298 K.
questions.answer:
$\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$. With solubility $x$ mol L$^{-1}$: $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]=x$, $[\text{OH}^-]=2x$.
$$K_{sp}=x(2x)^2=4x^3=6.4\times10^{-6}\Rightarrow x=\sqrt[3]{1.6\times10^{-6}}=1.17\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$
$M(\text{Ca(OH)}_2)=40.08+2(16.00+1.008)=74.096$ g mol$^{-1}$, so
$$\text{solubility}=1.17\times10^{-2}\times74.096=0.87\ \text{g L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
Using the information below, explain the effect a temperature increase would have on the quoted $K_{sp}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$.

| Thermodynamic data (25 °C, 100 kPa) | $\Delta H^\circ_f$ / kJ mol$^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| $\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)$ | $-543$ |
| $\text{OH}^-(aq)$ | $-230$ |
| $\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)$ | $-986$ |
questions.answer:
The dissolving reaction is $\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$.
$$\Delta H^\circ=\sum\Delta H^\circ_f(\text{products})-\sum\Delta H^\circ_f(\text{reactants})=[-543+2(-230)]-(-986)=-17\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}.$$
The dissolution is exothermic ($\Delta H<0$). By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which is to the left (towards solid $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$). The concentrations of the ions at equilibrium decrease, so the value of $K_{sp}=[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$ decreases and the solubility is lower at a higher temperature.

questions.question:
A change in the position of equilibrium can be demonstrated visually using two forms of cobalt(II) ions. Solutions of the $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ion are pink and solutions of the $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ ion are blue. A solution made from $0.5$ M $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ions and $5$ M $\text{Cl}^-$ ions reaches the following equilibrium:
$$\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(pink; colourless; blue). At room temperature, the mixture is blue when this solution is at equilibrium.

Write the equilibrium expression, $K_{eq}$, for the equation above.
questions.answer:
$$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$$
(Liquid water is not included.)

questions.question:
A change in the position of equilibrium can be demonstrated visually using two forms of cobalt(II) ions. Solutions of the $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ion are pink and solutions of the $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ ion are blue. A solution made from $0.5$ M $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ions and $5$ M $\text{Cl}^-$ ions reaches the following equilibrium:
$$\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(pink; colourless; blue). At room temperature, the mixture is blue when this solution is at equilibrium.

One 20 mL sample is diluted by adding 10 mL of deionised water at room temperature. The solution immediately becomes a paler blue due to the dilution. Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain the colour change expected from this paler blue colour until a new equilibrium is reached.
questions.answer: Dilution reduces the concentration of all dissolved ions, but it has a greater effect on the reactant side (5 dissolved particles, $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ and $4\text{Cl}^-$) than on the product side (1 dissolved particle, $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$). The system responds to oppose the change by shifting to the side with more dissolved particles, i.e. to the left, forming more pink $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ions and colourless $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. The solution therefore changes from pale blue towards pink (less blue) until a new equilibrium is established.

questions.question:
A change in the position of equilibrium can be demonstrated visually using two forms of cobalt(II) ions. Solutions of the $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ion are pink and solutions of the $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ ion are blue. A solution made from $0.5$ M $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ions and $5$ M $\text{Cl}^-$ ions reaches the following equilibrium:
$$\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(pink; colourless; blue). At room temperature, the mixture is blue when this solution is at equilibrium.

$10$ g of $\text{AgNO}_3$ crystals is mixed into a second 20 mL sample of the equilibrium mixture. What effect will the addition of $\text{AgNO}_3$ crystals to the second solution have on the position of equilibrium? Explain your answer in terms of collision theory. Write an ionic equation for the reaction involving $\text{AgNO}_3$.
questions.answer:
The $\text{AgNO}_3$ dissolves, and the silver ions react with chloride ions to form a white precipitate of silver chloride:
$$\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{AgCl}(s)$$
This removes $\text{Cl}^-$ from the equilibrium mixture, so the position of equilibrium shifts to the left. In terms of collision theory, with fewer chloride ions per unit volume there are fewer collisions per second between $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, so the rate of the forward reaction decreases, while the reverse reaction rate is initially unchanged. The reverse reaction therefore temporarily exceeds the forward reaction, forming more pink $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$, until the rates are equal again at a new equilibrium containing a smaller proportion of blue ions and a larger proportion of pink ions. (The equilibrium is not destroyed: only about $0.06$ mol $\text{Ag}^+$ is added, but about $0.10$ mol $\text{Cl}^-$ is present in $20$ mL.)

questions.question:
A change in the position of equilibrium can be demonstrated visually using two forms of cobalt(II) ions. Solutions of the $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ion are pink and solutions of the $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ ion are blue. A solution made from $0.5$ M $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$ ions and $5$ M $\text{Cl}^-$ ions reaches the following equilibrium:
$$\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(pink; colourless; blue). At room temperature, the mixture is blue when this solution is at equilibrium.

Samples of the original equilibrium solution are pink when refrigerated at $4^\circ$C and blue when kept at $25^\circ$C. Is the forward reaction in the original equilibrium solution endothermic or exothermic? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The forward reaction is **endothermic**. Increasing the temperature from $4^\circ$C to $25^\circ$C changes the solution from pink to blue, so the position of equilibrium shifts to the right, producing more blue $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$. By Le Chatelier's principle, an increase in temperature favours the endothermic direction (which absorbs heat and opposes the temperature rise). So the forward reaction, which forms the blue ion, absorbs heat. (In terms of collision theory, a higher temperature gives a greater proportion of particles with energy at or above the activation energy, which increases the rate of the endothermic reaction more than that of the exothermic reaction.)

questions.question: The structures of two organic compounds, $A$ and $B$, are shown: compound $A$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (the OH on the middle carbon) and compound $B$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Name compounds $A$ and $B$.
questions.answer: $A$ = propan-2-ol; $B$ = propanoic acid.

questions.question: The structures of two organic compounds, $A$ (propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) and $B$ (propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) are shown. Identify an isomer of $A$ which can be converted to compound $B$.
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (an isomer of propan-2-ol and a primary alcohol), which can be oxidised (e.g. by acidified permanganate or dichromate under reflux) to propanoic acid.

questions.question: Compound $A$ is propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$. Draw the structural formula of the organic compound, $C$, which is formed when compound $A$ is oxidised using acidified potassium dichromate solution, and name this compound.
questions.answer:
Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone. Compound $C$ is **propanone** (acetone):
$$\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{CH}_3$$
(a central carbon with a C=O double bond, each side bonded to a methyl group). Its structural formula has the carbonyl carbon bonded to two $\text{CH}_3$ groups and double bonded to O, with no H on the carbonyl carbon.

questions.question: A student heated $250$ g of water by combusting $1.8$ g of butanol. The starting temperature of the water was $23^\circ$C. Calculate the final temperature of the water if there is $20\%$ heat loss to the surroundings, given that the molar heat of combustion of butanol is $2871$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. (Specific heat capacity of water $=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; molar mass of butanol $74.12$ g mol$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
$n(\text{butanol})=\dfrac{1.8}{74.12}=0.0243$ mol.

Heat released: $q=0.0243\times2871=69.7$ kJ.

$20\%$ is lost, so heat absorbed by the water $=0.80\times69.7=55.8$ kJ $=55\,800$ J.

$$\Delta T=\frac{q}{mc}=\frac{55\,800}{250\times4.18}=53.4^\circ\text{C}$$
$$T_{final}=23+53.4=76^\circ\text{C}.$$

questions.question: Sodium fluoride forms a solution with a pH around $8.6$ when added to water, whereas amphiprotic sodium hydrogen sulfate forms a solution with a pH of $1$. Compare and contrast how each of these salts affects the pH of water.
questions.answer:
Both salts dissolve and dissociate completely into their ions, and in both cases the $\text{Na}^+$ ion is the cation of a strong base ($\text{NaOH}$) and does not react with water, so it does not affect the pH. In each case it is the anion that reacts with water in a Brønsted–Lowry proton-transfer reaction, and both anions are able to accept a proton from water; the difference is in the extent to which they do so.

**Sodium fluoride** is a basic salt. $\text{F}^-$ is the conjugate base of the weak acid $\text{HF}$, so it is a (weak) Brønsted–Lowry base and accepts a proton from water, producing hydroxide ions:
$$\text{F}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{HF}(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$$
The excess of $\text{OH}^-$ makes the solution slightly alkaline (pH about 8.6). Fluoride can only act as a base (it has no proton to donate).

**Sodium hydrogen sulfate** is amphiprotic: $\text{HSO}_4^-$ can both accept and donate a proton.
$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\quad(\text{acting as a base})$$
$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\quad(\text{acting as an acid})$$
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong acid, so its conjugate base accepts protons only to a negligible extent, whereas $\text{HSO}_4^-$ is a relatively strong acid ($K_a\approx1\times10^{-2}$). The acidic reaction therefore dominates in water, producing a high concentration of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and a strongly acidic solution (pH about 1).

**Similarity:** both anions react with water by proton transfer. **Difference:** fluoride acts only as a base and raises the pH (basic salt), whereas hydrogen sulfate, although amphiprotic, acts predominantly as an acid and lowers the pH (acidic salt).

questions.question: Using structural formulae, write a balanced equation for the production of an ester using acetic (ethanoic) acid and 1-propanol. Name the ester produced.
questions.answer:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\overset{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4}{\rightleftharpoons}\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
The structural formulae are: ethanoic acid $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{OH}$, propan-1-ol $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$, and the ester $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$ (the $-$OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol's $-$OH are lost as water).

The ester is **propyl ethanoate** (propyl acetate).

questions.question: Explain the conditions needed to efficiently and safely carry out the esterification of ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol in the school laboratory.
questions.answer:
- A few drops of **concentrated sulfuric acid** are added to the mixture of alkanol and alkanoic acid. The acid acts as a catalyst, increasing the rate at which the ester is produced, and as a dehydrating agent, removing water and so shifting the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of ester.
- The mixture is **heated** (to increase the reaction rate) using a hot water bath or heating mantle rather than a naked flame, because the alcohol and ester are volatile and flammable.
- The mixture is heated **under reflux** (using a condenser above the reaction vessel), which allows heating for an extended period without loss of volatile reactants and products and without a dangerous build-up of gas pressure that could cause an explosion (the vessel must not be sealed).

questions.question:
The table shows the boiling points of some organic compounds.

| Name | Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | Boiling point ($^\circ$C) |
|---|---|---|
| Acetic acid | 60.1 | 117.9 |
| Propan-1-ol | 60.1 | 97.2 |
| Ethyl methanoate | 60.1 | 54.2 |

Explain the difference in boiling points between these three compounds.
questions.answer:
The boiling point of a substance depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces between its molecules: stronger forces need more energy to overcome, giving a higher boiling point. The three compounds have the same molar mass, so dispersion forces are similar and the differences are due to polarity and hydrogen bonding.

Ethyl methanoate is an ester with no $-$OH group; its molecules are polar and have dipole–dipole attractions but cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, so it has the weakest forces and lowest boiling point. Propan-1-ol and acetic acid each contain an $-$OH group and can form hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are stronger, so they boil at higher temperatures. Acetic acid has a higher boiling point than propan-1-ol because its carboxyl group ($-$COOH) is more polar and the molecules form more extensive hydrogen bonding (including with a C=O oxygen, and dimers), giving the strongest intermolecular forces.

questions.question: During your study of chemistry, you performed an analysis to estimate the acid content in vinegar against sodium hydroxide by titration. Describe AND justify four steps you took in performing your analysis, to reduce experimental errors and thus ensure your titration results were valid and reliable.
questions.answer:
Any four of the following (step, with justification):

| Step taken | Justification |
|---|---|
| The burette was given a final rinse with the standardised NaOH solution | So the concentration of the NaOH is not altered by residual water when it is placed in the burette |
| The pipette was given a final rinse with the diluted vinegar solution | So the concentration of the vinegar sample is not altered by residual water in the pipette |
| The conical flask was rinsed with distilled water only | So the flask is clean, and the moles of acid delivered by the pipette are not changed (rinsing with the solution would add extra moles of acid) |
| The NaOH solution was standardised against a primary standard before use | NaOH is not a primary standard (it absorbs water and CO$_2$ from the air), so its concentration must be accurately known |
| Phenolphthalein indicator was used | Its colour-change range (pH 8.3–10) matches the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration (pH above 7) |
| The titration was repeated until concordant titres were obtained, and the average used | To increase reliability and reduce the effect of random error |
| A white tile or paper was placed under the conical flask | So the end-point colour change can be seen more easily and judged consistently |

questions.question: Citric acid, the predominant acid in lemon juice, is a triprotic acid. A student titrated $25.0$ mL samples of lemon juice with $0.550$ mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. The mean titration volume was $29.50$ mL. The molar mass of citric acid is $192.12$ g mol$^{-1}$. What was the concentration of citric acid in the lemon juice in g L$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaOH})=0.550\times29.50\times10^{-3}=0.016225$ mol.

Citric acid is triprotic (1 mol reacts with 3 mol NaOH): $n(\text{citric acid})=\dfrac{0.016225}{3}=5.408\times10^{-3}$ mol.

$$c=\frac{5.408\times10^{-3}}{25.0\times10^{-3}}=0.216\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
$$\text{concentration}=0.216\times192.12=41.6\ \text{g L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: Hydrogen iodide can be produced by the reversible reaction of hydrogen gas and iodine gas: $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$. $K_{eq}$ for this reaction is $2.25\times10^3$ at a temperature of $753^\circ$C. Calculate the concentration of HI in an equilibrium mixture if the concentration of $\text{H}_2$ is $0.15$ M and the concentration of $\text{I}_2$ is $0.25$ M.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}\Rightarrow[\text{HI}]=\sqrt{2.25\times10^3\times0.15\times0.25}=\sqrt{84.4}=9.2\ \text{M}.$$

questions.question: Hydrogen iodide can be produced by the reversible reaction $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$, for which $K_{eq}=2.25\times10^3$ at $753^\circ$C. $2.4$ mol of $\text{H}_2(g)$ and $1.5$ mol of $\text{I}_2(g)$ were placed in a sealed $2.0$ L vessel maintained at $753^\circ$C. After 2 hours, the amounts present were $1.7$ mol $\text{H}_2$, $0.8$ mol $\text{I}_2$ and $1.4$ mol HI. Show by calculation whether the forward or reverse reaction must increase for the system to come to a state of dynamic equilibrium.
questions.answer:
Concentrations: $[\text{HI}]=1.4/2.0=0.70$ M, $[\text{H}_2]=1.7/2.0=0.85$ M, $[\text{I}_2]=0.8/2.0=0.40$ M.
$$Q=\frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}=\frac{0.70^2}{0.85\times0.40}=1.44.$$
Since $Q=1.44<K_{eq}=2.25\times10^3$, the system is not at equilibrium and there is too little product relative to the equilibrium ratio, so the forward reaction must proceed at a faster rate than the reverse reaction (the forward reaction increases) until equilibrium is reached.

questions.question: E10 engine fuel is a blend of $10\%$ ethanol and $90\%$ petrol. One of the issues with its use is the absorption of water vapour from the atmosphere. Referring to its molecular structure, explain how ethanol is able to blend with petrol and also causes water retention in the fuel blend.
questions.answer: The ethanol molecule, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$, has both a polar $-$OH (hydroxyl) group and a non-polar $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-$ hydrocarbon chain. The non-polar chain can form dispersion forces with the non-polar hydrocarbon molecules of petrol, so ethanol is miscible (soluble) in petrol. The polar $-$OH group can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so ethanol attracts water and is also soluble in water. Hence ethanol acts as a solvent for both petrol and water, and the ethanol in E10 absorbs water vapour from the air and retains it in the fuel blend.

questions.question: E10 engine fuel is a blend of $10\%$ ethanol and $90\%$ petrol. Discuss the basis of the claim that ethanol as a fuel is carbon-neutral, and does not increase atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$.
questions.answer:
Ethanol, like petrol, produces carbon dioxide when burned: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(l)+3\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow2\text{CO}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$. However, ethanol is made by fermenting sugars from crops such as sugar cane or wheat, and the carbon in those plants was absorbed from the atmosphere as $\text{CO}_2$ during photosynthesis: $6\text{CO}_2(g)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)+6\text{O}_2(g)$. The $\text{CO}_2$ released when the ethanol is burned is therefore balanced by the $\text{CO}_2$ removed from the atmosphere as the crop grew, which is the basis of the claim that ethanol is carbon-neutral (unlike petrol, which releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years).

However, the claim ignores $\text{CO}_2$ produced elsewhere in the ethanol fuel cycle: in cultivating, fertilising, harvesting and transporting the crop, in the fermentation itself (which also produces $\text{CO}_2$), and in the energy needed to distil the ethanol, which is often obtained from burning fossil fuels. So the overall fuel cycle is not truly carbon neutral, although its net contribution to atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$ is lower than that of petrol.

questions.question: In a fermentation experiment, $6.50$ g of glucose was completely converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide. What is the mass of carbon dioxide produced?
questions.answer:
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$

$n(\text{glucose})=\dfrac{6.50}{180.16}=0.03608$ mol; $n(\text{CO}_2)=2\times0.03608=0.07216$ mol.

$m(\text{CO}_2)=0.07216\times44.01=3.18$ g.

questions.question:
A flow diagram shows a synthesis pathway starting from but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$: Step 1: reaction with HCl gives a compound; Step 2: but-1-ene is converted to butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; Step 3: butane reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ and UV light to give 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (+ HCl); Step 4: reaction with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ gives a compound; Step 5: that compound reacts with excess $\text{KMnO}_4$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; Step 6: the products of Steps 4 and 5 react with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give a compound.

Name and draw the structural formula for the compound formed in Step 1.
questions.answer: HCl adds across the C=C bond of but-1-ene. The H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (Markovnikov's rule), so Cl bonds to the second carbon. The product is **2-chlorobutane**, $\text{CH}_3-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$ (the Cl is on the second carbon of the four-carbon chain).

questions.question:
A flow diagram shows a synthesis pathway starting from but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$: Step 1: reaction with HCl gives a compound; Step 2: but-1-ene is converted to butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; Step 3: butane reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ and UV light to give 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (+ HCl); Step 4: reaction with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ gives a compound; Step 5: that compound reacts with excess $\text{KMnO}_4$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; Step 6: the products of Steps 4 and 5 react with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give a compound.

Name and draw the structural formula for the compound formed in Step 4.
questions.answer: 1-chlorobutane undergoes substitution with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ ($\text{OH}^-$ replaces $\text{Cl}^-$) to give **butan-1-ol**, $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$.

questions.question:
A flow diagram shows a synthesis pathway starting from but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$: Step 1: reaction with HCl gives a compound; Step 2: but-1-ene is converted to butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; Step 3: butane reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ and UV light to give 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (+ HCl); Step 4: reaction with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ gives a compound; Step 5: that compound reacts with excess $\text{KMnO}_4$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; Step 6: the products of Steps 4 and 5 react with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give a compound.

Give a chemical equation for the reaction involved in Step 5.
questions.answer:
Butan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) is oxidised by excess acidified permanganate to butanoic acid:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}+2[\text{O}]\xrightarrow{\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+}\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

questions.question:
A flow diagram shows a synthesis pathway starting from but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$: Step 1: reaction with HCl gives a compound; Step 2: but-1-ene is converted to butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; Step 3: butane reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ and UV light to give 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (+ HCl); Step 4: reaction with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ gives a compound; Step 5: that compound reacts with excess $\text{KMnO}_4$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; Step 6: the products of Steps 4 and 5 react with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give a compound.

Name and draw the compound formed in Step 6.
questions.answer: In Step 6 butan-1-ol (Step 4) and butanoic acid (Step 5) undergo esterification with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst. The product is **butyl butanoate**, $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$ (water is also formed).

questions.question:
To identify the three anions present in a solution, the following procedure was performed: a mixture of anions $A$, $B$ and $C$ had magnesium nitrate solution added and was filtered, giving a white precipitate $D$ and a clear solution. Hydrochloric acid added to $D$ gave bubbles of a colourless gas, $E$. Barium chloride solution was added to the clear solution and filtered, giving a white precipitate $F$ and a clear solution; lead nitrate solution added to this clear solution gave a yellow precipitate $G$.

Identify precipitate $D$ and gas $E$.
questions.answer: $D$ is magnesium carbonate, $\text{MgCO}_3$ (the carbonate anion is precipitated by $\text{Mg}^{2+}$). $E$ is carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$: $\text{MgCO}_3(s)+2\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(g)$.

questions.question:
To identify the three anions present in a solution, the following procedure was performed: a mixture of anions $A$, $B$ and $C$ had magnesium nitrate solution added and was filtered, giving a white precipitate $D$ and a clear solution. Hydrochloric acid added to $D$ gave bubbles of a colourless gas, $E$. Barium chloride solution was added to the clear solution and filtered, giving a white precipitate $F$ and a clear solution; lead nitrate solution added to this clear solution gave a yellow precipitate $G$.

Write net ionic equations for the formation of precipitates $F$ and $G$.
questions.answer:
$F$ (white, barium sulfate, so the second anion is sulfate): $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)$

$G$ (yellow, lead(II) iodide, so the third anion is iodide): $\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{I}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{PbI}_2(s)$

questions.question: A compound is known to be either calcium chloride or iron(III) chloride. Describe a simple test that could be used to distinguish between the two.
questions.answer: Dissolve a sample of each in water and add sodium hydroxide solution. Calcium chloride gives a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide, $\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)$ (and the solution is colourless), whereas iron(III) chloride gives a red-brown (rusty) precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)+3\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Fe(OH)}_3(s)$ (the iron(III) chloride solution is also yellow-brown before the test). (Other valid tests include a flame test: calcium gives a brick-red flame, whereas iron(III) gives no characteristic colour.)

questions.question: Explain why $0.1$ M solutions of sulfuric acid, acetic acid and hydrochloric acid have different pH values.
questions.answer:
- **Hydrochloric acid** is a strong monoprotic acid that ionises completely: $\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)$. $[\text{H}^+]=0.1$ M, so pH $=1$.
- **Acetic acid** is a weak monoprotic acid that ionises only partially: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)$. $[\text{H}^+]$ is much less than $0.1$ M (about $1.3\times10^{-3}$ M using $K_a=1.8\times10^{-5}$), so its pH is higher (about $2.9$).
- **Sulfuric acid** is a strong diprotic acid; each molecule can release two protons: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)\rightarrow2\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$ (treating both ionisations as complete). $[\text{H}^+]\approx0.2$ M, so pH $\approx0.7$ (in fact the second ionisation, of $\text{HSO}_4^-$, is not complete, so the actual pH is about $0.96$, still lower than that of HCl).

So the pH differs because of differences in the degree of ionisation (strong vs weak) and in the number of protons each acid can donate (monoprotic vs diprotic): pH of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4<$ HCl $<$ $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.
